claim: TWIST1 BioID-proximity-labeling and network propagation analyses discovered and characterized a TWIST-chromatin regulatory module (TWIST1-CRM) in neural crest cells (NCC).
source: Using TWIST1 BioID-proximity-labeling and network propagation analyses, we discovered and characterized a TWIST-chromatin regulatory module (TWIST1-CRM) in the neural crest cells (NCC).
evidence: The abstract directly states the methodology used and the discovery made.

claim: Combinatorial perturbation of TWIST1, CHD7, CHD8, and WHSC1 in cell models and mouse embryos resulted in abnormal differentiation of NCCs and compromised craniofacial tissue patterning.
source: Combinatorial perturbation of core members of TWIST1-CRM: TWIST1, CHD7, CHD8, and WHSC1 in cell models and mouse embryos revealed that loss of the function of the regulatory module resulted in abnormal differentiation of NCCs and compromised craniofacial tissue patterning.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the experimental approach and the observed phenotypic outcomes.

claim: Low level of TWIST1-CRM activity after NCC delamination stabilizes early NCC signatures and migratory potential by repressing neural stem cell programs.
source: Following NCC delamination, low level of TWIST1-CRM activity is instrumental to stabilize the early NCC signatures and migratory potential by repressing the neural stem cell programs.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes the functional role of low TWIST1-CRM activity.

claim: High level of TWIST1 module activity at later phases commits cells to the ectomesenchyme.
source: High level of TWIST1 module activity at later phases commits the cells to the ectomesenchyme.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the role of high TWIST1 activity in cell fate commitment.

claim: The study revealed functional interdependency of TWIST1 and potential neurocristopathy factors in NCC development.
source: Our study further revealed the functional interdependency of TWIST1 and potential neurocristopathy factors in NCC development.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this as a finding of the study.

claim: Mutations in TWIST1 in humans are associated with craniosynostosis.
source: As an example, mutations in transcription factor TWIST1 in human are associated with craniosynostosis (El Ghouzzi et al., 2000) and cerebral vasculature defects (Tischfield et al., 2017).
evidence: The text cites a reference supporting this association.

claim: Mutations in TWIST1 in humans are associated with cerebral vasculature defects.
source: As an example, mutations in transcription factor TWIST1 in human are associated with craniosynostosis (El Ghouzzi et al., 2000) and cerebral vasculature defects (Tischfield et al., 2017).
evidence: The text cites a reference supporting this association.

claim: TWIST1 is required in NCCs for the formation of the facial skeleton.
source: Phenotypic analyses of Twist1 conditional knockout mouse revealed that TWIST1 is required in the NCCs for the formation of the facial skeleton, the anterior skull vault, and the patterning of the cranial nerves (Soo et al., 2002; Ota et al., 2004; Bildsoe et al., 2009; Bildsoe et al., 2016).
evidence: The text cites multiple references supporting this requirement.

claim: TWIST1 is required in NCCs for the formation of the anterior skull vault.
source: Phenotypic analyses of Twist1 conditional knockout mouse revealed that TWIST1 is required in the NCCs for the formation of the facial skeleton, the anterior skull vault, and the patterning of the cranial nerves (Soo et al., 2002; Ota et al., 2004; Bildsoe et al., 2009; Bildsoe et al., 2016).
evidence: The text cites multiple references supporting this requirement.

claim: TWIST1 is required in NCCs for the patterning of the cranial nerves.
source: Phenotypic analyses of Twist1 conditional knockout mouse revealed that TWIST1 is required in the NCCs for the formation of the facial skeleton, the anterior skull vault, and the patterning of the cranial nerves (Soo et al., 2002; Ota et al., 2004; Bildsoe et al., 2009; Bildsoe et al., 2016).
evidence: The text cites multiple references supporting this requirement.

claim: NCCs arise from the neuroepithelium at the border with the surface ectoderm through pre-epithelial-mesenchymal transition (pre-EMT).
source: NCCs also arise from the neuroepithelium, at the border with the surface ectoderm through the pre-epithelial-mesenchymal transition (pre-EMT) which is marked by the activation of Tfap2a, Id1, Id2, Zic1, Msx1 and Msx2 (Baker et al., 1997; Mayor et al., 1997; Saint-Jeannet et al., 1997; Marchant et al., 1998; Etchevers et al., 2019).
evidence: The text cites multiple references supporting this developmental process.

claim: Pre-EMT in NCCs is marked by the activation of Tfap2a, Id1, Id2, Zic1, Msx1 and Msx2.
source: NCCs also arise from the neuroepithelium, at the border with the surface ectoderm through the pre-epithelial-mesenchymal transition (pre-EMT) which is marked by the activation of Tfap2a, Id1, Id2, Zic1, Msx1 and Msx2 (Baker et al., 1997; Mayor et al., 1997; Saint-Jeannet et al., 1997; Marchant et al., 1998; Etchevers et al., 2019).
evidence: The text cites multiple references supporting these molecular markers.

claim: Twist1 expression is initiated during NCC delamination.
source: Twist1 expression is initiated during NCC delamination and its activity is sustained in migratory NCCs to promote ectomesenchymal fate (Soldatov et al., 2019).
evidence: The text cites a reference supporting this temporal expression pattern.

claim: Twist1 activity is sustained in migratory NCCs to promote ectomesenchymal fate.
source: Twist1 expression is initiated during NCC delamination and its activity is sustained in migratory NCCs to promote ectomesenchymal fate (Soldatov et al., 2019).
evidence: The text cites a reference supporting this functional role.

claim: TWIST1 mediates cell fate choices through functional interactions with other basic-helix-loop-helix (bHLH) factors.
source: TWIST1 mediates cell fate choices through functional interactions with other basic-helix-loop-helix (bHLH) factors (Spicer et al., 1996; Firulli et al., 2005; Connerney et al., 2006) in addition to transcription factors SOX9, SOX10, and RUNX2 (Spicer et al., 1996; Hamamori et al., 1997; Bialek et al., 2004; Laursen et al., 2007; Gu et al., 2012; Vincentz et al., 2013).
evidence: The text cites multiple references supporting these interactions.

claim: TWIST1 mediates cell fate choices through functional interactions with transcription factors SOX9, SOX10, and RUNX2.
source: TWIST1 mediates cell fate choices through functional interactions with other basic-helix-loop-helix (bHLH) factors (Spicer et al., 1996; Firulli et al., 2005; Connerney et al., 2006) in addition to transcription factors SOX9, SOX10, and RUNX2 (Spicer et al., 1996; Hamamori et al., 1997; Bialek et al., 2004; Laursen et al., 2007; Gu et al., 2012; Vincentz et al., 2013).
evidence: The text cites multiple references supporting these interactions.

claim: BioID methodology captures TWIST1 interactions in the native cellular environment including transient and low-frequency events.
source: Leveraging the proximity-dependent biotin identification (BioID) methodology, we captured TWIST1 interactions in the native cellular environment including previously intractable transient and low-frequency events which feature interactions between transcription regulators (Roux et al., 2012; Kim and Roux, 2016).
evidence: The text cites references supporting the capabilities of BioID methodology.

claim: 140 putative TWIST1 interactors in NCCs were identified (p<0.05; Fold-change >3; PSM#>2).
source: Differential binding analysis of TWIST1 using sum-normalized peptide-spectrum match (PSM) values (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C; see Materials and methods) revealed 140 putative TWIST1 interactors in NCCs (p<0.05; Fold-change >3; PSM#>2; Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states the number of interactors identified and the statistical criteria used.

claim: TWIST1 BioID candidates included 4 of 56 known TWIST1 interactors: TCF3, TCF4, TCF12, and GLI3.
source: These candidates included 4 of 56 known TWIST1 interactors, including TCF3, TCF4, TCF12, and GLI3 (overlap odds ratio = 18.05, Chi-squared test p-value=0.0005; Agile Protein Interactomes DataServer [APID]) (Alonso-López et al., 2019; Fan et al., 2020).
evidence: The text explicitly lists the known interactors recovered and cites supporting references.

claim: The overlap of TWIST1 BioID candidates with known interactors has an odds ratio of 18.05 (Chi-squared test p-value=0.0005).
source: These candidates included 4 of 56 known TWIST1 interactors, including TCF3, TCF4, TCF12, and GLI3 (overlap odds ratio = 18.05, Chi-squared test p-value=0.0005; Agile Protein Interactomes DataServer [APID]) (Alonso-López et al., 2019; Fan et al., 2020).
evidence: The text explicitly provides the statistical measure of overlap significance.

claim: Biotinylated proteins in TWIST1-BirA* transfected cells were predominantly localized in the nucleus.
source: In the transfected cells, biotinylated proteins were predominantly localized in the nucleus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B; Singh and Gramolini, 2009).
evidence: The text references a figure showing nuclear localization and cites a supporting reference.

claim: The profile of TWIST1-BirA* biotinylated proteins was different from that of biotinylated proteins captured by GFP-BirA*.
source: The profile of TWIST1-BirA* biotinylated proteins were different from that of biotinylated proteins captured by GFP-BirA* (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The text references a figure showing differential protein profiles.

claim: Western blot analysis detected TCF4 among TWIST1-BirA* biotinylated proteins but not in the control group.
source: Western blot analysis detected TCF4, a known dimerization partner of TWIST1, among the TWIST1-BirA* biotinylated proteins but not in the control group (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The text references a figure showing Western blot results.

claim: Network propagation identified functional modules amongst novel TWIST1 BioID-interactors and prioritized key NCC regulators.
source: We invoked network propagation analytics to identify functional modules amongst novel TWIST1 BioID-interactors and to prioritize the key NCC regulators (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The text explicitly describes the analytical approach and its purpose.

claim: Gene Ontology analysis revealed major biological activities of proteins in the clusters: chromatin organization, cranial skeletal development, and ribosome biogenesis.
source: Gene Ontology analysis revealed major biological activities of proteins in the clusters: chromatin organization, cranial skeletal development, and ribosome biogenesis (Figure 1C; Supplementary file 2; Chen et al., 2009).
evidence: The text references a figure and supplementary file showing GO analysis results.

claim: CHD7, CHD8, PRRX1, PRRX2, and DVL1 interact with TWIST1 as shown by co-immunoprecipitation assays.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) assays showed that CHD7, CHD8, PRRX1, PRRX2, and DVL1 could interact with TWIST1 like known interactors TCF3 and TCF4, while TFE3 and SMARCE1 did not show any detectable interaction (Figure 2A).
evidence: The text references a figure showing co-IP results.

claim: TFE3 and SMARCE1 did not show detectable interaction with TWIST1 in co-IP assays.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) assays showed that CHD7, CHD8, PRRX1, PRRX2, and DVL1 could interact with TWIST1 like known interactors TCF3 and TCF4, while TFE3 and SMARCE1 did not show any detectable interaction (Figure 2A).
evidence: The text references a figure showing lack of interaction in co-IP.

claim: The p2 and p3 regions of CHD7 and CHD8 interacted with full-length TWIST1 and its N-terminal region.
source: In contrast, the p2 and the p3 regions of CHD7 and CHD8 interacted with full-length TWIST1 as well as with its N-terminal region (Figure 2C).
evidence: The text references a figure showing domain-specific interactions.

claim: CHD7, CHD8, and WHSC1 interacted preferentially with the TWIST1 N-terminus.
source: CHD7, CHD8, and WHSC1 interacted preferentially with the TWIST1 N-terminus whereas the TCF dimerization partners interacted specifically with the bHLH domain (Figure 2D).
evidence: The text references a figure showing domain-specific interactions.

claim: TCF dimerization partners interacted specifically with the TWIST1 bHLH domain.
source: CHD7, CHD8, and WHSC1 interacted preferentially with the TWIST1 N-terminus whereas the TCF dimerization partners interacted specifically with the bHLH domain (Figure 2D).
evidence: The text references a figure showing domain-specific interactions.

claim: The histone acetyltransferase CBP/P300 binds the TWIST1 N-terminal region.
source: Interestingly, the other known factor that binds the TWIST1 N-terminal region is the histone acetyltransferase CBP/P300 which is also involved in chromatin remodeling (Hamamori et al., 1999).
evidence: The text cites a reference supporting this interaction.

claim: Compound heterozygous embryos (Twist1+/-;Chd7+/-, Twist1+/-;Chd8+/-, and Twist1+/-;Whsc1+/-) displayed more severe craniofacial abnormalities and exencephaly than single-gene heterozygous embryos.
source: Compound heterozygous embryos (Twist1+/-;Chd7+/-, Twist1+/-;Chd8+/-, and Twist1+/-;Whsc1+/-) displayed more severe craniofacial abnormalities and exencephaly (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: The text references figures showing embryo phenotypes.

claim: Twist1+/-;Chd8+/- compound mutant embryos displayed expanded neuroepithelium, a phenotype not observed in single-gene mutants.
source: While Chd8+/- embryos showed incomplete neural tube closure, compound Twist1+/-;Chd8+/- embryos displayed expanded neuroepithelium, a phenotype not observed in the single-gene mutants (Figure 3B,E).
evidence: The text references figures showing the expanded neuroepithelium phenotype.

claim: The population of NCCs expressing Tfap2α was reduced in the frontonasal tissue and the trigeminal ganglion of Twist1+/-;Chd8+/- embryos.
source: The population of NCCs expressing Tfap2α, a Twist1-independent NCC marker (Brewer et al., 2004) was reduced in the frontonasal tissue and the trigeminal ganglion (Figure 3E–i,F).
evidence: The text references figures showing reduced Tfap2α expression.

claim: SOX2 expression was upregulated in the ventricular zone of the neuroepithelium of Twist1+/-;Chd8+/- mutant chimeras.
source: In contrast, SOX2 expression was upregulated in the ventricular zone of the neuroepithelium of mutant chimeras (Figure 3E–ii,iii,G).
evidence: The text references figures showing upregulated SOX2 expression.

claim: Twist1+/-, Chd8+/- and Twist1+/-;Chd8+/- embryos displayed different degrees of hypoplasia of the NCC-derived cranial nerves.
source: Furthermore, Twist1+/-, Chd8+/- and Twist1+/-;Chd8+/- embryos displayed different degrees of hypoplasia of the NCC-derived cranial nerves (Figure 3H).
evidence: The text references a figure showing cranial nerve defects.

claim: Cranial nerves III and IV were absent in Twist1+/-;Chd8+/- compound mutant embryos.
source: Cranial nerves III and IV were absent, and nerve bundle in the trigeminal ganglia showed reduced thickness, most evidently in the Twist1+/-;Chd8+/- compound mutant embryos (Figure 3H,I).
evidence: The text references figures showing absent cranial nerves.

claim: Nerve bundle in the trigeminal ganglia showed reduced thickness in Twist1+/-;Chd8+/- compound mutant embryos.
source: Cranial nerves III and IV were absent, and nerve bundle in the trigeminal ganglia showed reduced thickness, most evidently in the Twist1+/-;Chd8+/- compound mutant embryos (Figure 3H,I).
evidence: The text references figures showing reduced nerve bundle thickness.

claim: TWIST1 genetically interacts with epigenetic regulators CHD7, CHD8, and WHSC1 to guide the formation of the cranial NCC and downstream tissue genesis in vivo.
source: Altogether, these results suggested that TWIST1 genetically interaction with epigenetic regulators CHD7, CHD8, and WHSC1 to guide the formation of the cranial NCC and downstream tissue genesis in vivo.
evidence: The text explicitly states this conclusion based on the genetic interaction studies.

source: Genome-wide co-occupancies of TWIST1, CHD7, and CHD8 showed significant overlap (Fisher's exact test) and clustered by Jaccard Similarity matrix (Figure 4A).

source: ChIP-seq peaks were correlated with active histone modifications H3K27ac and H3K4me3 but not the inactive H3K27me3, or the WHSC1-associated H3K36me3 modifications (Figure 4A).
evidence: The text references a figure showing correlation with histone modifications.

claim: TWIST1 shared 63% of target genes with CHD8 (odds ratio = 16.93, Chi-squared test p-value<2.2e-16).
source: TWIST1 shared 63% of target genes with CHD8 (odds ratio = 16.93, Chi-squared test p-value<2.2e-16) and 18% with CHD7 (odds ratio = 8.26, p-value<2.2e-16; Figure 4B; Supplementary file 4).

claim: TWIST1 shared 18% of target genes with CHD7 (odds ratio = 8.26, p-value<2.2e-16).
source: TWIST1 shared 63% of target genes with CHD8 (odds ratio = 16.93, Chi-squared test p-value<2.2e-16) and 18% with CHD7 (odds ratio = 8.26, p-value<2.2e-16; Figure 4B; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The text explicitly provides the statistical measure of target gene overlap.

claim: Genomic regions with peaks for two or all three factors (TWIST1, CHD7, and CHD8) showed greater percentage of H3K27ac and H3K4me3 signal compared to regions occupied by only one factor.
source: Compared with genomic regions occupied by only one factor, greater percentage of regions with peaks for two or all three factors (TWIST1, CHD7, and CHD8) showed H3K27ac and H3K4me3 signal (Figure 4C).

source: Similarly, the co-occupied transcription start sites (TSS) showed open chromatin signatures with enrichment of H3K4me3 and H3K27Ac and depletion of H3K27me3 (Ernst et al., 2011; Rada-Iglesias et al., 2011; Figure 4D,E).

source: While Chd7+/-, Chd8+/-, and Whsc1+/- mutant cells displayed marginally reduced motility, the motility of the Twist1+/- cells was compromised and further reduced in Twist1+/-; Chd7+/-, Twist1+/-; Chd8+/-, and Twist1+/-; Whsc1+/- compound mutant cells (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: The text references figures showing cell migration assay results.

source: Impaired motility in Twist1, Chd8 and Whsc1 knockdowns was accompanied by reduced expression of EMT genes (Snail2, Ddr2, Pcolce, Pdgfrb, Mmp2) and ectomesenchyme markers (Prrx1, Prrx2, Foxc1, Snai1; Figure 6D).
